title: Two accounts hitting a target, on a sorted book
prompt:
The book of business arrives **already sorted ascending by premium**. An underwriter
wants exactly two accounts whose premiums add up to a target.

Return the **indices** `[i, j]` with `i < j`, or `[]` if no pair works. An account
cannot pair with itself.

If several pairs work, return the outermost one: the smallest `i`, and with it the
largest `j`.

```
sorted_pair_sum([1000, 2500, 3000, 4500, 7000], 7000) -> [1, 3]
sorted_pair_sum([1500, 1500, 3000], 3000)             -> [0, 1]
sorted_pair_sum([1000, 2000], 5000)                   -> []
```

Use **O(1) extra space**. A dict solves this too, and that is the wrong answer here.

### Why this one
This is Two Sum with the sort already done for you, and it is asked precisely to see
whether you notice. An interviewer is listening for one sentence -- "it is sorted, so I
can converge two pointers and drop the hash map" -- and then for whether you can say
*why* moving a pointer is safe. Candidates who have only memorised the dict version
write the dict version, and the follow-up ("now do it in constant space") is where the
round goes quiet.
hints: You already solved this with a dict. That costs O(n) space. What does the input being sorted let you rule out that an unsorted input would not?
Put one pointer at each end. If the two premiums add up to too little, the only way to increase the sum is to move the left pointer right; if too much, move the right pointer left.

while lo < hi: total = a[lo] + a[hi]; equal -> return [lo, hi]; total < target -> lo += 1; total > target -> hi -= 1. Note `lo < hi`, not `lo <= hi` -- with `<=` the two pointers can land on the same element and pair it with itself.
explanation:
### Why moving a pointer is safe
This is the sentence that separates "I remember the trick" from "I understand it", and
it is worth rehearsing:

> If `a[lo] + a[hi] < target`, then `a[lo]` paired with **anything** still in the window
> is also too small, because `a[hi]` is the largest thing left. So `lo` has no partner
> and can be discarded forever.

The mirror argument retires `hi`. Each step throws away exactly one index and never
throws away a valid pair, so one pass is enough and the answer, if it exists, survives
until the pointers reach it.
followups: Return every distinct pair that hits the target, not just one. (Same walk; on a hit, record it and then skip past the duplicate values on both sides before continuing.)

The list is not sorted. Which solution wins? (Sort first: O(n log n) time, O(1) space, but it destroys the original indices. The dict is O(n) time and O(n) space and keeps them. Say the trade-off rather than picking one.)
Three accounts summing to a target. (Fix the first with an outer loop, run this two-pointer scan on the rest: O(n^2).)

python.notes:
### Ruby to Python notes
- `lo, hi = 0, len(premiums) - 1` is parallel assignment, same as Ruby. On an empty list `hi` is `-1`, the loop never runs, and you get `[]` for free -- no empty guard needed.
- There is no `+=` on integers in the Ruby sense of mutation: `lo += 1` rebinds the name. Fine here, but it means you cannot mutate an int through a function call the way you might expect.
- Do **not** reach for `while lo <= hi`. Python will happily let `lo == hi` and `premiums[lo] + premiums[hi]` will double one element, returning `[2, 2]` on input like `[1000, 2000, 4000]` with target 8000. The answer there is `[]`.
- Tempted by `premiums.index(target - p)`? It is O(n) per call and returns the *first* match, which is the wrong tie-break and quietly turns this into O(n^2).

javascript.notes:
### Ruby to JavaScript notes
- `premiums.length - 1` on an empty array is `-1`, the loop never runs, and `[]` falls out. No empty guard needed -- but note that `premiums[-1]` would be `undefined` rather than the last element, so never lean on negative indices the way Ruby lets you.
- Use `===`, not `==`. `==` coerces, so `0 == "0"` and `0 == []` are both true; on a JSON-decoded feed where a premium arrived as a string that is a real bug, not a hypothetical one.
- **Nothing is returned implicitly.** The trailing `return []` is load-bearing: falling off the end gives `undefined`, which is not an empty array and will fail every no-pair test.
- `indexOf` is the reflex a Rubyist reaches for in place of `index`, and it is O(n) per call. Using it inside the loop turns a linear scan into a quadratic one without looking any different.

### Why moving a pointer is safe
If `a[lo] + a[hi] < target`, then `a[lo]` paired with anything still in the window is also
too small, because `a[hi]` is the largest thing left -- so `lo` has no partner and can be
discarded forever. The mirror argument retires `hi`. Each step throws away exactly one
index and never throws away a valid pair.

complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Sorting first, if the input were unsorted, would make it O(n log n).
